vignette:
Vera's Vigilance

Vera Kovalenko was seventy-four, with silver hair she kept in a neat braid and the careful posture of someone who had spent a lifetime teaching others how to move through their bodies without pain. She had been a physical therapist for forty-three years, first in Prague and then, after 1968, in the United States. Her hands were steady; her mind, these days, was not. She had come to her first appointment carrying a folder of intake forms filled in with meticulous handwriting, each answer precise and controlled, as if precision itself might keep the past at bay.

The trauma that had shaped Vera's life had occurred in August 1968, when she was just twenty-six. Soviet tanks had rolled into Czechoslovakia, and in the chaos of those first nights, Russian soldiers had forced their way into the apartment building where she lived with her parents. She had hidden in a storage closet while her mother pleaded with the men in the hallway. The sounds—the heavy boots on wooden floors, the rough voices shouting in Russian, the crash of furniture being overturned, the smell of alcohol on breath and sweat—had burned themselves into her nervous system with the intensity of a brand. She had escaped Prague two months later, eventually making her way to America, where she had built a careful, controlled life. But the past, she had come to understand, was not something you could outrun simply by crossing an ocean.

Now, seven decades later, Vera found herself trapped in a cycle she could not seem to interrupt. Certain moments would pull her back into that closet with startling force. When her husband mentioned the anniversary of the invasion—or worse, when someone at a dinner party asked her to talk about her experiences—Vera would feel the memory descend like a physical weight. The conversation itself became a trigger; talking about what had happened would flood her mind with vivid images of the hallway, the soldiers' faces, the narrow darkness of the closet. Over time, she had simply stopped accepting dinner invitations, and when family gatherings approached, she would find reasons to stay home—not consciously avoiding the memory, but recognizing, with a kind of grim certainty, that the only way to prevent the flood was to remove herself from situations where the past might be asked to speak. Those images, when they came, felt utterly present. She was not remembering 1968; she was living it. The memory had no temporal boundary. It was happening now, in her living room in Connecticut, while her husband sat beside her with concern in his eyes. When the vividness became unbearable—when the hallway seemed to materialize around her in the middle of an ordinary afternoon—Vera had learned that only movement and distraction could break the grip; she would turn on the television at high volume, or find tasks that demanded her full attention, anything to drown out the internal noise that threatened to pull her under.

The sensory details were the most treacherous. A whiff of alcohol—whiskey at a restaurant, or someone's cologne that carried that sharp, fermented note—would trigger not just the image but the full sensory flood. But even before the memory surfaced, the smell itself sent a jolt of danger through her body; her heart would quicken, her muscles would tense, and she would feel certain that something catastrophic was about to unfold, as if the cue itself were a warning her nervous system had learned to read as an emergency. She would hear, in her head, the slurred Russian voices, the sound of breaking glass, the heavy breathing of men moving through rooms. Her body would respond as if the danger were immediate and real. The smell of something burnt—toast left too long in the toaster, leaves smoldering in a neighbor's yard—would send her into a state of acute vigilance, convinced that something was wrong, that danger was present in a form she could not yet identify.

These moments of triggered memory had slowly reshaped how Vera moved through the world. She had begun to scan her environment constantly, listening for sounds that might indicate someone entering her home. At night, she would lie awake, her attention fixed on the creaks of the house settling, the distant sound of a car passing on the street, the hum of the refrigerator—each noise parsed for threat. When she was at her clinic, seeing patients, she found herself acutely aware of male clients who approached from behind, even though she knew intellectually that the young man with a rotator cuff injury posed no danger to her. Yet her body did not believe what her mind knew. She would tense, her breath would shallow, and she would react as if she were in imminent danger, even when nothing was actually wrong.

To manage the anxiety that had become her constant companion, Vera had begun drinking in the evenings. A glass of wine became two, then three. She told herself it was simply to help her sleep, to quiet the vigilance that kept her awake. Yet the alcohol itself deepened her sense of threat rather than relieving it; the taste and smell of it would resurrect the very sensations she was trying to escape, and each drink seemed to confirm, in her body's logic, that danger was real enough to require numbing. But the alcohol itself was a trigger—the taste, the smell, the way it loosened her defenses—and each drink seemed to make the memories more vivid rather than less so. She found herself dwelling on how she used to be before the invasion, before the fear had taken root. She would think about the young woman she had been, confident in her body, unafraid in her own home, and the loss of that version of herself would compound the original trauma into something almost unbearable.

The checking, the scanning, the constant threat assessment—these had become as automatic as breathing. Yet they seemed to deepen her sense of danger rather than relieve it. Each time she scanned the room and found nothing, she would think, Not yet. The danger is still out there. Because she never stayed in a moment long enough to feel genuinely safe—never sat with the "all-clear" signal long enough for her body to truly believe it—the threat remained as vivid and immediate as it had been fifty-six years ago; the very behaviors that were meant to protect her had sealed off any possibility of learning that the danger had passed. Her threat system, sensitized by decades of unprocessed trauma, had become hyperactive, seeing peril in ordinary moments. The more she drank to quiet it, the more vivid her memories became. The more vivid the memories, the more she felt the need to check, to scan, to monitor. The cycle had tightened around her until she could barely distinguish between what was real and what was a echo from fifty-six years ago.

It was her husband who finally insisted she seek help. He had found her one morning sitting in the kitchen at three a.m., a glass of wine in her hand, listening to the house. She had told him she thought someone was trying to get in. He held her hand and said, quietly, that she could not keep living like this. Vera, looking at the fear in his eyes—fear for her, not of her—had finally agreed. What she wanted most was to feel safe in her own home again. What she feared most was that the person she had been before the tanks came would never return.
